newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine economy growing but analysts wary of overheating.
newsitem.headline: Philippine economy growing but analysts wary of overheating.

text.p: Solid growth in the first nine months of 1996 and an expected increase in investments have boosted the Philippines' hopes of becoming Asia's newest Tiger.
But analysts warned on Sunday against dangers that could burst the bubble.

Spurred by an agricultural rebound, record remittances from overseas workers and a construction boom, gross national product grew by 7.1 percent in the first three quarters versus 5.3 percent in the same period a year ago, officials said on Saturday.
"With this kind of growth, we are going towards the direction of becoming a tiger economy," said Kenneth Nerecina, research director of Vickers Ballas Securities Phils Inc.
But businessmen said the government should be vigilant for signs of overheating.

"The economy is now a new born tiger (but) we have to think ahead and learn from the experiences of our tiger neighbours," Raul Concepcion, president of the Federation of Philippine Industries, told Reuters.
Besides diversifying its exports to reduce reliance on traditional products, the government should put a "dampener" on the real estate boom, Concepcion said.
"All over the world, we have seen so many workers displaced when their real estate bubble burst," he warned.
Industries should also make their products more competitive as trade barriers in the region begin to crumble, Concepcion said.
"The name of the game is lowest cost and better quality," he said.

Socioeconomic Planning Secretary Cielito Habito said he expected the economy to sustain its growth for the rest of the year and predicted 1996 GNP would probably hit 7.2 percent, well above earlier projections of 6.5 percent.

But University of the Philippines economics professor Benjamin Diokno was not impressed. He said that without the strong agricultural growth and a rise in workers' remittances from abroad, "the picture of the economy is one which is slowing down."

Noting that industry grew at a slower pace of 6.2 percent from 7.4 percent, Diokno added: "This suggests that unless the overseas remittances continue to flow, the foreign exchange needed to finance the country's investment needs may not be forthcoming."
The Central Bank projects remittances from four million Filipinos working abroad to hit $7 billion this year.

President Fidel Ramos, in a statement, said the economic uptrend should be further boosted by "the expected influx of foreign investments" following the success of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit held in the country last week.
Philippine government and private firms signed joint venture deals worth more than $2 billion during the APEC meetings.

Concepcion said investments, which would go mostly to infrastructure, would further strengthen the economy. "But the country needs to generate more foreign exchange to pay off these investments," he said.

Philippine gross domestic product grew by 5.9 percent in third quarter of 1996 - the highest quarterly growth rate since fourth quarter of 1989, when GDP grew by 7.5 percent. GDP is GNP less foreign income.
Economists attributed the GDP growth to the liberalisation of the banking, telecommunications and power sectors.
Ramos, who recently signed a peace deal with mainsteam Moslem rebels on resource-rich Mindanao island, also predicted the southern region would play a big role in the country's economic growth.
"(Mindanao) is the region to watch," he said. "I urge you to invest your money in Mindanao. I assure you, they will multiply."
